items.title: 人类在 AI 辅助软件开发中应扮演何种角色？
items.raw_excerpt: Martin Fowler 博客中，Kief Morris 探讨了 AI 辅助开发中人的角色，认为开发者不会完全脱离开发流程，未来更多会以 “在循环之上” 的模式工作，通过制定规范、测试与反馈机制来指导 AI 智能体，而非逐一审查 AI 生成的内容。

title_i18n.zh: 人类在 AI 辅助软件开发中应扮演何种角色？
title_i18n.en: What role should humans play in AI-assisted software development?
title_i18n.es: ¿Qué papel debe desempeñar el ser humano en el desarrollo de software asistido por IA?

excerpt_i18n.zh: Martin Fowler 博客中，Kief Morris 探讨了 AI 辅助开发中人的角色，认为开发者不会完全脱离开发流程，未来更多会以 “在循环之上” 的模式工作，通过制定规范、测试与反馈机制来指导 AI 智能体，而非逐一审查 AI 生成的内容。
excerpt_i18n.en: In Martin Fowler's blog, Kief Morris discusses the role of humans in AI-assisted development, arguing that developers will not be completely removed from the development process. Instead, they will increasingly work in an "over the loop" mode, guiding AI agents by setting standards, tests, and feedback mechanisms, rather than reviewing each piece of AI-generated content individually.
excerpt_i18n.es: En el blog de Martin Fowler, Kief Morris analiza el papel de los humanos en el desarrollo asistido por IA, argumentando que los desarrolladores no se desvincularán completamente del proceso de desarrollo. En el futuro, trabajarán más en un modelo "sobre el bucle", guiando a los agentes de IA mediante la definición de estándares, pruebas y mecanismos de retroalimentación, en lugar de revisar minuciosamente cada contenido generado por la IA.

excerpt_i18n.en: On March 18, a price increase announcement from Alibaba Cloud stirred waves in the cloud computing industry. More significant than the "price hike" itself, however, was the signal it sent: after years of price wars, cloud providers have begun systematically passing cost pressures to the market for the first time. That same afternoon, Baidu Intelligent Cloud quickly followed suit; earlier, AWS, Google Cloud, UCloud, and Tencent Cloud had already raised their prices. Thus, an AI-driven "computing power price surge" has resonated globally. "If we don’t raise prices, costs will become unsustainable," an industry insider long focused on the cloud sector told Leifeng.com. Over the past year, the explosion of AI applications has pushed demand for computing power to unprecedented heights, while supply—including GPU capacity, data centers, and electricity—has struggled to keep pace. With demand growing exponentially and supply still constrained by physical limits, price has become an inevitable variable. Notably, this is not a uniform price increase. Facing similar cost pressures, different domestic cloud providers are making divergent choices: some are adjusting only AI-related services while leaving core offerings untouched, others are implementing across-the-board hikes, and some are holding prices steady, aiming to capture market share through competitive pricing. "If we don’t raise prices, everyone’s costs will become unsustainable." "Everyone in the industry knew this wave of price increases was inevitable," cloud sales representative Zhang Xiangyu told Leifeng.com. In his view, this is not an active choice by cloud providers but rather a passive adjustment. Changes on the demand side are the most direct driver.
excerpt_i18n.es: El 18 de marzo, un anuncio de aumento de precios de Alibaba Cloud causó revuelo en la industria de la computación en la nube. Sin embargo, lo más importante no es el "aumento de precios" en sí, sino la señal que emite: después de años de guerra de precios, los proveedores de servicios en la nube están comenzando por primera vez a transmitir sistemáticamente la presión de costos al mercado. Esa misma tarde, Baidu Intelligent Cloud respondió rápidamente; antes, AWS, Google Cloud, UCloud y Tencent Cloud ya habían ajustado sus precios gradualmente. Así, una "ola de aumento de precios en la capacidad de cómputo", impulsada por la IA, ha generado una resonancia global. "Si no subimos los precios, realmente no podremos soportar los costos", afirmó un profesional del sector que sigue de cerca la industria de la nube a Leifeng.com. excerpt_i18n.en:
At the start of this year, global software stock investors collectively experienced a "terrifying sixty days." From the end of last year to the beginning of this year, the market was still immersed in the illusion of an "AI application explosion." However, at the end of January, Anthropic unveiled Claude Cowork, capable of autonomously operating computers and handling office tasks, which directly shattered the valuation logic of traditional SaaS. In just two months, North American software stocks lost over $1.6 trillion in market value. A nearly desperate sentiment pervaded the market: if AI can already operate computers and take over business workflows like humans, have the graphical interfaces and business software painstakingly built over the past two decades become outdated productivity tools? Addressing these life-or-death questions, in an online roundtable hosted by Leiphone GAIR Live, three industry veterans with deep expertise in SaaS and complementary perspectives—He Run: Co-founder and CEO of Zhi Qu Bai Chuan; Daniel: Senior investor and business head at a major internet company; Wu Hao: Author of "SaaS Entrepreneurship Roadmap," angel investor in leading SaaS companies, and former executive president—engaged in a rigorous 90-minute dialogue, offering penetrating insights into the current state and future of SaaS.  
1. Recent Plunge in SaaS Stock Prices: Not Due to Financial Revenue, but Expectations Being Dimensionality-Reduced  
In Daniel's view, the sharp decline in SaaS is not due to SaaS companies' financial data falling short of expectations, but rather expectations being subjected to a dimensionality-reducing blow.
excerpt_i18n.es: A principios de este año, los inversores en acciones de software a nivel global experimentaron juntos una "aterradora sesenta días". Desde finales del año pasado hasta principios de este, el mercado aún estaba inmerso en la ilusión de la "gran explosión de aplicaciones de IA". Sin embargo, a finales de enero, Anthropic lanzó Claude Cowork, capaz de operar computadoras de forma autónoma y realizar tareas de oficina independientes, lo que directamente destrozó la lógica de valoración del SaaS tradicional. En solo dos meses, las acciones de software en Norteamérica perdieron más de 1.6 billones de dólares en valor de mercado. El mercado se impregnó de un discurso casi desesperado: si la IA ya puede operar computadoras como un humano y hacerse cargo de los flujos de negocio, entonces, ¿para qué sirven las interfaces gráficas y los procesos comerciales que hemos construido con tanto esfuerzo en las últimas dos décadas?

items.title: Gemini can now natively embed video, so I built sub-second video search
items.raw_excerpt:
Gemini Embedding 2 can project raw video directly into a 768-dimensional vector space alongside text. No transcription, no frame captioning, no intermediate text. A query like "green car cutting me off" is directly comparable to a 30-second video clip at the vector level. I used this to build a CLI that indexes hours of footage into ChromaDB, then searches it with natural language and auto-trims the matching clip. Demo video on the GitHub README.
Indexing costs ~$2.50/hr of footage. Still-frame detection skips idle chunks, so security camera / sentry mode footage is much cheaper.

Over the past month, the global tech scene has been turned upside down by a "lobster" named OpenClaw. It directly reads and writes local files, autonomously controls desktop applications, breaks down complex tasks, and works for you. Following OpenClaw, major tech companies have rolled out their own AI work assistants. From an application perspective, the current mainstream AI agents globally mostly serve as personal assistants in office settings, remaining at the "Copilot" stage—they excel at handling documents, organizing spreadsheets, and summarizing notes, essentially acting as "interns" working for humans.

However, business owners, especially small and medium-sized enterprises and individual entrepreneurs overseas, face a different reality: communication delays due to time zones, unreliable product selection data, the tedious complexity of multi-platform operations, and the nerve-wracking process of supply chain negotiations. Beyond this, they have higher demands for security and reliability, yet these more complex needs remain unmet. They urgently desire an easy-to-use agent.

Accio Work has precisely addressed these pain points. On March 23, Alibaba quietly dropped a depth charge in the overseas market with the official launch of its first enterprise-level agent for international markets—Accio Work. In the simplest terms, Accio Work is Alibaba’s enterprise-level business intelligence agent designed for overseas small and medium-sized enterprises and individual entrepreneurs, deploying a 24/7 "digital workforce" to help them start companies and run businesses.
